title: The speed of belonging
dek: Give people a trivial label and a little rivalry, and a we appears. The trick is almost embarrassingly fast.
speakingPrompts: Describe a group you joined in under a day. What was the smallest shared badge?
How would you design a classroom activity that builds belonging without inventing an enemy?
When is fast belonging a gift, and when is it a trap?

blocks.text: Henri Tajfel’s minimal-group experiments remain a cold splash of water. Strangers sorted by a coin toss or a preference for a painter will still favour “their” side in the allocation of points. They know the groups are made up. They still tilt. Belonging does not require a mythic past. It requires a line and a chance to stand on one side of it.
Why the mind is so eager

Categories reduce social uncertainty. Once you have a we, you can predict a little, borrow status, and outsource some of your self-definition. The same machinery that lets a choir form in an afternoon lets a comment section find a scapegoat. Speed is the feature. You do not have time, in evolutionary terms, to run a full background check on every coalition.

Modern life exploits the feature constantly: shirts, slogans, schools, software fandoms. None of these are automatically sinister. A team needs a boundary or it is a crowd. The ethical question is what the boundary is for, and whether it needs an out-group to stay vivid. Rivalry is a cheap consolidator. Shared work is a slower one, and usually kinder.

blocks.title: A practical test
blocks.text: If your group vanished, would you miss the people, the craft, or the feeling of being against someone? The answer is information about what you actually joined.

You cannot uninstall coalitional thinking. You can notice the moment a label starts doing your reasoning for you. Pause before you allocate the points — praise, suspicion, the benefit of the doubt. Belonging will still happen at speed. Judgement does not have to.

references.title: The Social Identity Theory of Intergroup Behavior
references.source: Tajfel, H., & Turner, J. C. (1979). In Austin & Worchel (eds.), The Social Psychology of Intergroup Relations.
